questions.question: Why does getLine's type mention IO at all, instead of simply being String?
options: IO is just a naming convention with no real meaning
getLine cannot know what text it will produce until a real user types something at a real keyboard — that dependency on the outside world is exactly what IO marks in the type
IO String means the same thing as String, just written more formally
getLine :: IO String means it returns a list of Strings
questions.explanation: A pure Haskell value like a String literal is fixed once and for all by the source code. getLine cannot be like that — its result depends on what the user types, which varies at run time and involves the outside world. IO in the type is the signal that the value is obtained through an effect, not computed purely.
optionFeedback: IO carries real meaning: it marks a type as describing an action that interacts with the world outside the program, as distinct from a pure value.
IO String and String are different types entirely — an IO String is an action that can produce a String, not a String itself. That distinction is the whole point of this section.
IO String is one action producing one String result; it is unrelated to list types such as [String].

questions.question: A student writes `doubled <- number * 2` inside a do block. What is wrong, precisely?
options: Nothing; <- and let are interchangeable in a do block
number * 2 is a pure Integer expression, not an IO action, and <- requires its right side to be an action to perform — this needs let instead
doubled is not a valid variable name
number was never defined, so the line is meaningless regardless of <- or let
questions.explanation: <- is specifically for performing an IO action and capturing its result. number * 2 does not describe any interaction with the outside world — it is a pure calculation that already has a definite value. The correct form is let doubled = number * 2.
optionFeedback: They are not interchangeable: <- performs an IO action, let names a pure expression. Using the wrong one for the wrong side is a type error.
doubled is a perfectly ordinary identifier; the problem is the choice of <- rather than let, not the name itself.
This question is about the syntax choice between <- and let assuming number is already bound; that is a separate, real issue but not the one being tested here.

questions.question: After `let number = 4` and then `let doubled = number * 2`, what does `number` refer to?
options: 8, because doubled's definition changed it
Still 4 — let creates a new named binding (doubled) without modifying the existing one (number)
It becomes undefined once doubled is created
It depends on which line runs last in the program
questions.explanation: Haskell bindings are immutable. let doubled = number * 2 reads the current value of number to compute a brand new value and gives that new value its own name, doubled. It has no mechanism for reaching back and changing what number means.
optionFeedback: number is never modified by defining doubled; only doubled receives the new value 8.
number remains a valid, unchanged binding for as long as it is in scope — defining another name never invalidates it.
Binding order matters for what is in scope, but once number is bound to 4, no later let can change that binding — Haskell has no reassignment.

check-what-do-actually-desugars-to.title: Check: what do actually desugars to

questions.question: In getLine >>= \inputText -> restOfBlock, what exactly is restOfBlock?
options: A completely separate program that happens to run afterward
The remainder of the do block, written as the body of a function whose one parameter is the name to the left of the arrow, inputText
A comment describing what getLine does
An error-handling fallback in case getLine fails
questions.explanation: That is precisely what the desugaring shows: everything after inputText <- getLine in the original do block becomes the body of the lambda \inputText -> .... inputText is that function's parameter, which is exactly why every line after the <- can use it, and no line before it could.
optionFeedback: It is not separate at all — it is nested inside the >>= call, as the function that receives getLine's result.
Correct. This is the entire mechanism: each later statement becomes the body of a function taking the earlier binding as its parameter.
Nothing here is a comment; -- and {- -} are the only comment forms, and this is ordinary, executable desugared code.
This particular pattern is about sequencing and naming a result, not about error handling; >>= does not catch failures here.

questions.question: Why can the final putStrLn in the DoubleNumber program use doubled, number, AND inputText all at once, but inputText <- getLine could never have used doubled?
options: Because Haskell allows any binding to be used anywhere in the same file, regardless of order

Because each binding opens a new, deeper level of nesting that everything written afterward sits inside of; a name can only be seen by code nested inside the point where it was introduced, never by code written before it
Because doubled happens to be a shorter name than inputText
Because putStrLn has special permission to see every binding in the program
questions.explanation: The nesting diagram above shows exactly this: each statement is the body of a function nested inside the previous one. Being nested inside a scope is what makes a name visible; inputText <- getLine is not nested inside doubled's let, so it cannot see doubled — the nesting only goes one direction.
optionFeedback: Order matters a great deal — that is the entire point of the nesting structure; nothing here is a whole-file free-for-all.
Correct. This is the general rule stated directly: visibility follows nesting, and nesting only goes one direction — inward, not backward.
Name length has no bearing on scope; a one-letter name and a thirty-letter name follow exactly the same nesting rule.

putStrLn is an entirely ordinary function; it has no special scope privileges. It can see doubled only because the line calling it is textually nested inside doubled's let, like every other line in this block.

questions.question: Why does `read "4"` need the annotation `:: Integer` (or `:: Double`) to be usable, rather than Haskell just picking a type on its own?
options: Because "4" is not valid input for read without an annotation
Because read's result type is determined by what the caller asks for; the same text "4" could validly become an Integer, a Double, or another Read type, so the annotation resolves that ambiguity
Because :: Integer changes the string "4" into the character '4'
The annotation is purely optional style and never changes the result
questions.explanation: read :: Read a => String -> a is polymorphic in its result type — nothing about the string "4" by itself says whether the intended result is 4 :: Integer or 4.0 :: Double. Without other context forcing a specific type, GHC needs the annotation to know which Read instance to use.
optionFeedback: "4" is valid input for read; the issue is not validity but which result type to parse it as.
The annotation affects only the type of the Haskell value produced by read, not the string being parsed — read "4" always starts from the same three characters.
The annotation is exactly what determines the result here — try read "4" :: Integer versus read "4" :: Double and compare the two outputs shown above.

questions.question: In the trace above, step 5 says the original binding number still refers to 4 even after doubled is computed. Why is this true?
options: Because let bindings in Haskell are immutable — computing doubled reads number's value but cannot change what number itself is bound to
Because number and doubled are actually the same binding under two names
It is only true because the user entered a small number; larger numbers would change number
Because doubled is computed before number in the actual execution order
questions.explanation: Every let in this program introduces a brand-new, separate, immutable binding. number = 4 and doubled = number * 2 are two independent names; computing the second reads the first's value without any ability to alter it. This is the same immutability point made earlier in the lesson, now shown inside a full execution trace.
optionFeedback: They are two distinct bindings with two distinct values (4 and 8) — number and doubled are not aliases for the same thing.
The size of the number entered has no bearing on whether number can be mutated; Haskell bindings are immutable regardless of the value.
The do block's statements run in the written order: number is bound (step 4) strictly before doubled is computed (step 5).

questions.question: A student says: "the program stores the doubled number so I can use it later, even after the program exits." Which meaning of "store" does `let doubled = number * 2` actually provide, and does it satisfy that claim?
options: It provides persistent external storage, so the claim is correct
It provides only an immutable binding, which exists solely while the program is running; the claim is false — nothing here survives after the program exits
It provides a data structure, which is why it survives
It provides a source file, since the binding is written inside DoubleNumber.hs
questions.explanation: let doubled = number * 2 is an immutable binding: a name meaningful only within the running program's current scope. It vanishes the moment the program ends. Surviving the program's exit requires the fourth meaning — persistent external storage, using IO to write to a file or similar — which this lesson does not yet do.
optionFeedback: Persistent external storage requires an explicit IO write to something outside the process, such as a file; a let binding does no such thing.
doubled is a single Integer value bound by let, not a data structure like a list or tuple, and even a data structure would not survive the program ending on its own.
The binding lives inside the running program's memory, not as text in the source file — the source file's persistence (as saved text) is a different meaning from the binding's lifetime while running.

deeper-reasoning-input-binding-and-conve.title: Deeper reasoning: input, binding, and conversion

questions.question: GHC rejects the program below with the message that there is no instance for Num String arising from a use of +. The student believes the problem is the let keyword and tries replacing it with <-. Which diagnosis is the most accurate, and what is the correct repair?
options: let is the wrong form here; replacing it with <- fixes the problem because + is an IO operation.

ageText is a String, because getLine always produces text, even when the user types digits. + needs a numeric type, and String has no Num instance. The repair is to parse the text first, for example let age = read ageText :: Integer and then let nextYear = age + 1. let is still the correct form, because both lines are pure calculations.
The problem is the show in the last line, which cannot convert numbers to text.
getLine should be replaced by read, because read both waits for input and produces a number.
questions.explanation: Input arrives as text. Arithmetic needs numbers. The step between them is conversion, and read performs it, with the result type chosen by an annotation. Neither <- nor a change to show helps, because the error is about the type of ageText.
optionFeedback: <- requires an IO action on its right, and ageText + 1 is a pure calculation. Using it here would produce a different error and would not address the real problem.
Correct. The message is about the type of ageText: text cannot be added to a number. Converting with read, then calculating with let, is the pipeline the lesson builds.
show correctly converts the finished number to text for ++. The error occurs one line earlier and is about adding to a String.
read does not wait for input or perform any action. It only converts text that already exists, so it cannot replace getLine.

questions.question: A classmate studies the program below and says: "greeting is computed from name, which came from the keyboard, so it must also be bound with <-." Which reply best explains which operator belongs on each line and why?
options: The classmate is right: anything that depends on keyboard input is itself an IO result, so every later binding must use <-.
Both operators are interchangeable here, so the choice is purely a matter of taste.

<- is used on the getLine line because getLine is an IO action to perform and its result must be captured. The greeting line is a pure calculation on a String that already exists, so it only needs a name, which let provides. Where a value came from does not change whether the later calculation is pure.
let should be used for name as well, because a let binding can capture the result of any action.
questions.explanation: <- performs an action and binds its result. let names the value of a pure expression. The question to ask on each line is what is on the right-hand side: an action to run, or an expression to evaluate. Once the text exists, joining strings is an ordinary calculation.
optionFeedback: Dependence on earlier input does not turn a later calculation into an action. ++ never touches the outside world, so there is nothing to perform.
They are not interchangeable. Each one has a precondition about its right-hand side, and violating it is a type error.
Correct. The two lines show the two forms side by side: performing an action, then naming a pure value computed from its result.
let name = getLine would bind the action itself, not the text it produces, so name would have type IO String and could not be joined to a String.

questions.question: A program asks for a whole number, and the user types four instead of 4. The program stops with an exception whose message contains Prelude.read: no parse. A student concludes: "getLine is broken" and a second student suggests changing the annotation to :: Double. Which assessment is correct?
options: Both students are right: getLine cannot read words, and Double accepts spelled-out numbers.

Neither is right. getLine did its job and produced the text four. read could not interpret those characters as an Integer, and it has no way to recover, so the program stops. Changing the type to Double does not help, because four is not a valid Double either. Handling invalid text needs input validation, which this lesson defers until the required types have been taught.
The first student is right: getLine should reject non-numeric text before it returns.
The second student is right: read accepts any word if the annotation names a type with decimals.
questions.explanation: getLine only obtains a line of text, whatever it contains. Interpreting the text is read's job, and read assumes the text is valid for the requested type. Failure at that point is a run-time exception, not a type error, because the type of the program is perfectly correct.
optionFeedback: Neither claim holds: getLine returns any text without judging it, and no numeric type reads spelled-out words.
Correct. The fault is in the data, the conversion cannot recover, and the safer design is a separate validation step.
getLine has no idea what the text will be used for, so it cannot reject non-numeric characters. Checking belongs to a later step.
A different numeric type still needs digits. The word four is not valid for Integer, Double or any other numeric Read instance.
